newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian stocks detract 1.7 points from GDP.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian stocks detract 1.7 points from GDP.

text.p: Growth in Australian private non-farm inventories (stocks) detracted 1.7 percentage points from March quarter growth in GDP, a much larger detraction than the 0.5 percentage points that economists typically expected, analysts said.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics, which issued the data on Thursday, revised down its stocks contribution for the December quarter by 0.1 or 0.2 percentage points. The three quarters to December taken together lost 0.1 points in revisions.

The huge March quarter detraction, finally meeting economists' long-standing concerns over the stock build-up, occurred because the rate of stock accumulation dropped from A$625 million in the December quarter to minus A$1.293 billion in the March quarter.
That swing amounted to 1.7 percent of GDP.
"The Treasury can now say bye-bye to its forecast of 3.25 percent year-average GDP forecast for 1996/97 (to June)," said Access Economic director Chris Richardson.
Almost all of the massive fall in inventory accumulation had occured in the retail and wholesale industries, he said.

Inventory data has confounded economists for more than two years. A big lift in the rate of accumulation appeared at the end of 1994 and economists have been waiting nervously since then for it to unwind, especially since new business practises increasingly emphasise smaller inventories.
Many had given up waiting by the time this data appeared.

HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said the pattern of falling stocks in manufacturing, wholesaling and retailing was "back-up confirmation of the strong private consumption we've seen in the first quarter, and it acts now as a good stimulus to production looking forward to Q2 and Q3."

Inventory accumuluation is a component of the expenditure-based estimate of GDP. This estimate, GDP-E, is averaged with income and production-based estimates (GDP-I and GDP-P) to produce GDP-A, which is the focus of economic policy.
At minus 1.7 percentage points, the stocks contribution was about 1.2 points weaker than economists expected.
But since GDP-E has only a one-third weight in GDP-A, the effect on GDP-A forecasts should be minus 0.4 percentage points.

Thursday's inventory data is not complete, because it excludes farm and public authority stocks, but economists expect little impact from that sector when the March quarter GDP data is issued next Wednesday.
